title: 12  Typed Answers
text:
12.10 Next Steps
Part IV ends with the fast lane built and fenced. Part V returns to the slower senses, pictures and voice, where the payload grows a new kind of evidence and the clock starts charging rent. Readers headed for the optional Part VI may also proceed there directly; its notebooks assume Parts I and IV, not Part V.

title: 13  Pictures
text:
13.1 The Concept First
Package companion: hands_on_ai.vision, its one function describe. Listings checked against hands-on-ai 0.6.0.
Misconception this chapter kills: “Vision is a different kind of AI.” Images go into the same kind of call, and descriptions come out.
The build: talking-picture, the package’s vision project. A photograph that answers questions about itself, asked three different ways.
Python you need: one function call and a file path. The interesting work in this chapter is choosing photographs that test the model honestly.
A vision-language model, VLM for short, accepts a payload whose user message carries two parts instead of one string: your text question, and an image. Somewhere inside the server, the image is converted into tokens, the same internal units the model uses for words, and the machinery from Chapter 1 proceeds as always. Text and a picture go in, and text comes out. The module docstring puts it plainly: seeing is another way of writing a prompt. This module describes images. It does not create them; image generation is a different family of models and outside this book.
How the image travels explains the costs and failures to come. A web address can pass through as a link for the server to fetch. A local file, the normal case for your own photographs, is read by your code and encoded as base64, a text representation of the file’s bytes, inlined into the payload as a data URL. Your photograph becomes a long string inside the JSON from Chapter 1: a phone photograph inflates into hundreds of thousands of characters of payload before the server has done any thinking, which is one reason vision calls are slower and the package allows them a generous timeout.

title: 13  Pictures
text:
13.2 Understanding Through Real Life
Think of describing a scene over the phone to someone who has never seen your street. The description is a translation, and like every translation it is shaped by the question asked. “What is happening in this photo?” earns a story about the scene. “How many people are wearing hats?” earns a count the describer may or may not have performed carefully. “What does the sign say?” earns a reading, accurate where the sign is legible and confabulated where it is not, unless the describer is the rare sort who says the text is too small to read.
A VLM is that describer with two exaggerations. It has seen vastly more photographs in training than any person, and its scene sense is correspondingly strong. And it shares the language model’s reluctance to say it cannot tell: fine print, exact counts, small text, spatial relations like left-of versus behind, and anything the downscaled encoding smeared away may all come back rendered in fluent certainty. Chapter 5’s rule applies unchanged, with pixels added: separate what the image could show from what this call could recover, and check the parts that matter against the picture yourself.

title: 13  Pictures
section: 13.3 Connect a Vision Model Before You Build
text:
13.3 Connect a Vision Model Before You Build
Vision needs a model that accepts images, configured separately from your chat model, the way Chapter 6 added an embedding model. The default is moondream, a small vision model, changeable through the vision_model setting or HANDS_ON_AI_VISION_MODEL:
ollama pull moondream
handsonai doctor
The doctor reports the vision model alongside the others. If you point the package at a hosted provider instead, use one of its vision-capable models under the same setting; Appendix B gathers the details. Expect the first call to be slow while the model loads, and expect quality to track model size more than chat did. A small local VLM teaches well and proofreads poorly.

title: 13  Pictures
section: 13.4 The Build: a Photograph That Answers
text:
13.4 The Build: a Photograph That Answers
The module has one function, and its defaults need no help. Save a photograph of your own beside the script, something with a scene in it rather than a screenshot, and ask it three questions of widening difficulty:
# Listing 13.1 of 2: the talking picture (talking_picture.py)
from hands_on_ai.vision import describe

photo = "market.jpg"

print(describe(photo))
print(describe(photo, "What is the main thing being sold here?"))
print(describe(photo, "How many people are in this picture? Count carefully."))
The first call uses the default prompt, “Describe this image.”, and gets you the tour. The second shows the usual pattern: questions put to a picture, such as reading a label, identifying a plant, checking whether a gauge is in the red, or asking what is funny here. A picture plus a pointed question is the vision equivalent of Chapter 5’s grounded prompt, with the image as the evidence in the room. The third call is the honesty test. Counting is where small vision models go to be humbled, along with small text and precise spatial claims, and your own model may produce a crisp number you can refute by looking at the photograph.
Underneath, describe assembles the two-part user message and sends it through the same chat_completion machinery as every chat call in the book, with the longer timeout. One behaviour will look familiar from Chapter 1 by design: point it at a file that does not exist and you get an error string back, ❌ Error: Image file not found: ..., rather than a crash. Your program can tell failure from description the way it learned to in Part I.

title: 13  Pictures
section: 13.5 What It Can and Cannot See
text:
13.5 What It Can and Cannot See
A useful first hour with a VLM sorts its answers into three piles. Scene gist is strong: what kind of place this is, what is broadly happening, the salient objects and their rough relations. Reading is conditional: signage and labels come back well when they are large, level, and high-contrast, and degrade into plausible invention as they shrink, tilt, or blur. Precision work is weak on small models especially: exact counts, small differences between similar objects, charts read to values, and anything depending on detail the encoding downscaled away. Results vary with model size, and re-sorting the piles per model is the same moderation exercise Chapter 11 taught, with the photograph as ground truth sitting right there.
Vision output is text, so it can be judged: a description can be scored against criteria, and better, against a human transcript of the same image, by the machinery of Chapter 11. And a picture rarely answers the question behind the question alone. What the sign says comes from the photograph; whether the shop is open now comes from a document or a tool. Systems that pair a VLM’s description with retrieval from Chapter 6 or a lookup tool from Chapter 7 combine this book’s parts on one bench.






WarningPhotographs carry people



Your photographs will be uploaded, encoded, to whatever server your configuration names, and Chapter 3’s transcript warning applies with faces in place of words. Local models keep the bytes on your machine; hosted ones are governed by the provider’s retention terms. Photographs of other people deserve the consent habit you would want applied to your own likeness, and some workplaces and jurisdictions regulate biometric uses well beyond anything in this chapter. Description for learning is benign. Build the consent reflex anyway, while the stakes are homework.

title: 13  Pictures
section: 13.6 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
text:
13.6 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
Vision demos choose photographs the way Chapter 5’s demonstrators chose questions: big subjects, clean light, legible signs, counts of three. The counter-demo takes a minute to assemble from your own phone. A crowd to count, a receipt to read to the cent, a dashboard at an angle, a shelf where one item differs from its neighbours. Run the product on your photographs and sort its answers into this chapter’s three piles. Then ask the vendor’s questions: at what resolution is my image downscaled before the model sees it, where do the bytes go and how long are they kept, and show me the runs where the count was wrong. The pile boundaries will move as models grow, so draw them yourself, per model, on your material.

title: 13  Pictures
text:
13.7 Practice Exercises
Exercise 13.1 (Level 1). Run the talking picture on a photograph of your own. Ask the tour question and two pointed ones, and grade each answer against the picture.
Exercise 13.2 (Level 2). Assemble a five-photograph test set spanning the three piles: a scene, a sign or label, a crowd, a chart or receipt, a near-duplicate pair. Record where your model’s pile boundaries actually fall.
Exercise 13.3 (Level 3). Ask a question the photograph cannot answer (when it was taken, what happened next, who these people are). Record whether the model declines, hedges, or improvises, and compare with Chapter 5’s escape-sentence experiment.
Exercise 13.4 (Level 4). Pair the senses: describe a photograph of a document, save the description, and ask your Chapter 6 RAG bot a question needing both the picture’s content and your documents. Where did the hand-off between them lose information?
Exercise 13.5 (Level 5). Write the acceptance test for a vision feature at your workplace: the photograph set, the questions, the accuracy bar per pile, the consent and retention rules. One page, ending with the pile you would refuse to ship at this model’s scores.

title: 13  Pictures
text:
13.8 Chapter Summary

A vision call is a chat call whose user message carries text plus an image, inlined as base64 for local files. Descriptions come out; images are not created.
describe needs a vision-capable model, configured separately (moondream by default), and runs slower with a generous timeout. Missing files return an error string.
Sort your model’s work into scene gist (strong), reading (conditional on size and clarity), and precision (weak, especially counting and small text), using your own photographs as truth.
Vision output is text and composes with the rest of the book: it can be judged, grounded against documents, and checked like any other claim.
Photographs travel to the configured server. Local models keep them home; people in pictures deserve a consent habit.

title: 13  Pictures
text:
13.9 Reflection
Before moving on, ensure you:

Asked one photograph three questions of widening difficulty
Caught at least one fluent error by checking against the picture
Can say where your model’s three pile boundaries fall today
Know which server your photographs were sent to, and approve of it

title: 13  Pictures
text:
13.11 Next Steps
Pictures arrived as an attachment to the call you already had. Voice arrives the same way, twice over: one call turns speech into the text your chat loop already eats, and another turns its reply back into speech. The next chapter stitches those three calls into a conversation you can hear, and meets the one problem text never had, which is time.

title: 14  Voice
text:
14.1 The Concept First
Package companion: hands_on_ai.voice, with transcribe and speak, around the Conversation from Chapter 3. Listings checked against hands-on-ai 0.6.0.
Misconception this chapter kills: “Voice AI is a different technology.” It is transcribe, think, speak: three plain calls, and a fight against the clock.
The build: a talk-out-loud chatbot in two forms: typed input with spoken replies first, then a recorded question carried the whole way around the loop.
Python you need: function calls and the Conversation object. The new material is about servers and timing, not syntax.
The thinking in a voice system is the text machinery of Parts I to IV, unchanged, with two translators at the edges. A speech-to-text model, STT, takes an audio file and returns the words as text. That text enters the chat loop you built in Chapter 3 and receives a reply in text. A text-to-speech model, TTS, takes the reply and returns an audio file. That gives the loop: transcribe, think, speak. Each translator is a model call to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint under /v1/audio/, made with the same client patterns as Chapter 1 and Chapter 6’s embeddings. Voice adds senses the way pictures did: by converting to and from the text the system already runs on.
What changes is the constraint. Text chats tolerate a slow reply gracefully; the words appear when they appear. Spoken conversation runs on human turn-taking clock, where a pause of two seconds already feels like the other party has wandered off. Every hop in the chain spends from that budget: recording and uploading the audio, transcribing it, thinking over a growing transcript, synthesising the reply, downloading and playing it. Latency, the total time from the end of your sentence to the start of the reply, is the engineering problem of voice systems.

title: 14  Voice
text:
14.2 Understanding Through Real Life
Think of a conversation conducted through two interpreters in a soundproof booth relay. You speak your language. The first interpreter renders it into the booth’s working language and passes the words across. Your counterpart, who thinks in the working language, composes a reply. The second interpreter renders the reply back into yours. Everyone in the chain can be excellent and the conversation can still feel drunk, because each hand-off adds delay and small translation choices: a name heard slightly wrong enters the working language as fact, and a long, clause-heavy reply that reads beautifully becomes punishing when someone has to speak it and someone else has to stand there listening.
Transcription errors propagate inward disguised as the user’s own words, and the system answers the sentence it heard rather than the one you said. Reply style propagates outward: length, lists, tables, and URLs that serve a reader well become unusable when spoken, which is why voice system prompts beg for brevity.

title: 14  Voice
section: 14.3 Two More Servers Before You Build
text:
14.3 Two More Servers Before You Build
Audio models usually do not live on the chat server. A plain Ollama install serves chat, embeddings, and vision, but speech typically comes from a separate local server that speaks the same /v1/audio/ dialect: tools such as speaches or whisper.cpp serving Whisper models for transcription, and Kokoro or Piper for synthesis. The package therefore carries separate settings, HANDS_ON_AI_STT_SERVER and HANDS_ON_AI_TTS_SERVER, which default to your main server, and separate model settings defaulting to whisper-1 for transcription and kokoro for speech. A hosted provider with audio endpoints collapses all of this back to one address and one key, at hosted prices and with your voice recordings travelling to it.
Before building anything, point those settings at servers you actually have, local or hosted, and confirm with the doctor habits from Chapter 4. Appendix B collects the variables in one table. Then test the two translators in isolation, in the spirit of Chapter 7’s call-the-tool-yourself rule:
# Listing 14.1 of 2: the ears and the mouth, separately (voice_pieces.py)
from hands_on_ai.voice import speak, transcribe

print(speak("The loop is transcribe, think, and speak.", out_path="hello.wav"))
print(transcribe("hello.wav"))
speak returns the path of the WAV file it wrote, speech.wav in the current folder if you do not name one, or the familiar error string in place of the path. Empty text comes back as a warning string without troubling any server, Chapter 1 manners again. Feed the file it just made back through transcribe and you have run a small experiment: a sentence that went text to speech to text, with both translators at their best behaviour, on clean synthesised audio. Compare the returned words with the originals. Then transcribe a recording of yourself, made on your phone in a real room, and compare again. No chat model downstream can recover words the transcription missed.

title: 14  Voice
section: 14.4 The Build: the Loop Wearing Headphones
text:
14.4 The Build: the Loop Wearing Headphones
The package’s own interactive voice loop starts with a sensible cheat: you type what you would say, and only the reply is spoken. Microphone capture is platform plumbing, left as an extension exercise. In your own code it is Chapter 3’s Conversation with one added line, plus a system prompt that knows its output will be heard rather than read:
# Listing 14.2 of 2: typed question, spoken answer (voice_chat.py)
from hands_on_ai.chat import Conversation
from hands_on_ai.voice import speak

SYSTEM = (
    "You are a helpful assistant. Keep your answers short and "
    "conversational, one or two sentences, because they will be read aloud."
)

chat = Conversation(system=SYSTEM)

question = transcribe("my_question.wav") if False else input("You: ")
reply = chat.ask(question)
print(reply)
print(speak(reply, out_path="reply.wav"))
Flip the if False, record your question as a WAV file by whatever tool your machine offers, and the same script runs the full round trip, ears included, with Conversation still holding the transcript between turns if you wrap it in a loop of your own. Playback of the reply file is deliberately your problem; the package’s command-line REPL makes a best effort with afplay on macOS and aplay on Linux and otherwise tells you to open the file. That seam, getting sound out of speakers and in from microphones across operating systems and browsers, is where small demos end and voice frameworks like Pipecat begin, and Appendix D points at the bridge project, the package’s Build the World’s Smallest Pipecat.
Time one full turn with a stopwatch: question finished, reply audible. Then ask where the seconds went. Transcription of a short clip, the chat call over a transcript that grows every turn (Chapter 3’s tax, now audible), synthesis of the whole reply before the first sound plays. The industry’s answers are all visible from here: stream the reply in pieces and start speaking the first sentence while the rest generates, keep spoken answers short by instruction, run smaller local models for the translators, and put the servers close. None of those change the shape; they shorten the relay.






NoteVoice is biometric in a way text is not



A voice recording identifies a person in ways a typed sentence does not, and speech synthesis can be pointed at imitation with enough samples. The consent reflex from Chapter 13 applies in full: record yourself freely, record others with their knowledge, know which server your audio travelled to, and treat cloning a real person’s voice as a line that needs their explicit agreement rather than your technical ability. The tools in this chapter synthesise a stock voice. Keep the ethics at stock settings too.

title: 14  Voice
section: 14.5 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
text:
14.5 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
Voice demos are staged in quiet rooms with close microphones, short questions, and presenters who have learned to pause where the demo needs them to. Your counter-demo is a kitchen with a kettle on, a name the transcriber will mangle, a question whose honest answer is a list, and an interruption mid-reply. What is the end-to-end latency at the ninety-fifth percentile, not the anecdote? Where does my audio go, how long is it kept, and is it used for training? What happens when transcription hears me wrong: can I see the words the system thinks I said and correct them before action is taken? And which parts of this are your engineering, versus three API calls I assembled this morning from a learning package?

title: 14  Voice
text:
14.6 Practice Exercises
Exercise 14.1 (Level 1). Run voice_pieces.py, then transcribe a phone recording of the same sentence. Diff the two transcripts and list what the room cost you.
Exercise 14.2 (Level 2). Run the typed voice chat for four turns. Note the first reply that would have been fine on screen and was painful aloud, and adjust the system prompt because of it.
Exercise 14.3 (Level 3). Time a full round trip with a recorded question. Attribute the seconds across transcription, thinking, and synthesis as best you can, then shorten the turn by one deliberate change and re-time.
Exercise 14.4 (Level 4). Feed the loop its own transcription errors on purpose: dictate names, numbers, and a homophone-rich sentence. Where did the chat model recover the meaning anyway, and where did it earnestly answer the wrong sentence?
Exercise 14.5 (Level 5). Spec a voice front end for your Chapter 6 document bot: input and output paths, latency budget per hop, the spoken style rules, what the user sees when transcription is uncertain, and the consent and retention terms for recordings. One page, ending with the turn length at which you would switch the user back to text.

title: 14  Voice
text:
14.7 Chapter Summary

A voice agent is transcribe, think, speak: an STT call turns audio into text, the existing chat machinery answers, and a TTS call turns the reply into an audio file. All three are OpenAI-compatible calls.
Audio usually needs its own servers and models, configured separately with defaults falling back to the main server. speak returns a file path or an error string, and empty text is refused locally.
Latency is the voice problem: every hop spends from a turn-taking budget, and long replies hurt twice, once to generate and once to hear. Voice system prompts demand brevity for engineering reasons.
Transcription errors enter disguised as the user’s words, and the system answers the sentence it heard. Show the transcript where it matters.
Voice recordings are identifying data. Consent, retention, and refusing imitation are part of the build, not the brochure.

title: 15  The Older AI in the Room
text:
15.1 The Concept First
Notebook companion: classical_ml.ipynb in the package repository’s notebooks/ folder. It needs only scikit-learn, already installed as a package dependency, and runs in seconds with no model server of any kind.
Misconception this chapter kills: “AI means LLMs now.” The field is older and wider, and for a large class of tabular problems the older machinery is cheaper, clearer, and better behaved than a language model will ever be.
The build: a decision tree classifying iris flowers from four measurements, read back as plain rules and scored on sealed rows; then the labels thrown away and k-means left to find the groups alone.
AI is the umbrella: machines doing tasks we would call intelligent in a person. Under it sit several families with different ancestries. Symbolic AI reasons over rules and search. Classical machine learning fits models to tables: rows of examples, columns of numeric features, and, for supervised learning, a label to predict. Deep learning fits neural networks with gradient descent, the machinery the next chapter opens, and gave us both convolutional networks (CNNs) that learned to see images as spatial patterns and, eventually, the transformers behind LLMs. The first five parts of this book lived in that last twig of the family tree. This chapter visits the trunk it grew from, because the trunk still carries enormous weight: spam filtering, fraud scoring, demand forecasting, medical risk scores, and recommendation plumbing run overwhelmingly on classical models and their ensembles, as the 150-flower example below shows.
The classical workflow follows a rhythm: assemble a table, seal some rows away for testing before any fitting begins, fit a model on the rest, predict on the sealed rows, and evaluate against the truth you withheld: fit, predict, evaluate. Every later chapter in this part, including the adapter work with its sealed eval set, is that rhythm at greater expense.

title: 15  The Older AI in the Room
text:
15.2 Understanding Through Real Life
Think of a botanist’s field key, the printed kind that walks you through a plant by measurements. If the petal is under two and a half centimetres, it is a setosa; otherwise check the width; otherwise check this. A good key is a decision tree written by a person over seasons of observation. The notebook’s first build asks what key the data writes for itself when an algorithm chooses the thresholds to best separate the rows it was shown. The second build removes the guide’s species labels entirely and asks a different field question: given only measurements, do these flowers fall into natural groups at all? That is clustering, and its ancestor is every market segmentation and anomaly hunt running quietly in industry: find the lumps in the data first, argue about their names second.

title: 15  The Older AI in the Room
section: 15.3 The Build: a Key the Data Writes Itself
text:
15.3 The Build: a Key the Data Writes Itself
Open classical_ml.ipynb and run it top to bottom; this section narrates what to look at. The dataset is the iris table that ships inside scikit-learn, so nothing downloads: 150 flowers, four measurements each, three species in equal numbers. Thirty percent of rows are sealed away stratified by species, leaving 105 training rows and 45 test rows. Fitting is one line, DecisionTreeClassifier(...).fit(X_train, y_train), and it is over before you can look up. After five parts of server round trips, token budgets, and timeouts, a model that trains in milliseconds on your own CPU and needs no account, key, or network is a useful reminder that “AI” did not always imply a data centre.
Then print the model. The learned key opens with the same observation a botanist would, that petal length alone separates setosa cleanly (petal length (cm) <= 2.45), and resolves the harder two species through a handful of further width thresholds, eight leaves deep at most. Every prediction the tree ever makes can be traced down those branches by a person with a ruler. Scored on the sealed rows, the run captured for this draft (seed fixed, so yours should match) reaches 0.933 accuracy: 42 of 45 correct, with all three mistakes calling borderline versicolor flowers virginica. Read the mistakes individually, as the notebook does. Their measurements sit where the two species genuinely overlap, which is a property of flowers rather than a scandal in the model, and deciding whether those three errors matter is a judgement no accuracy number makes for you, as Chapter 11’s moderation sessions also show.
The second build deletes the answer key. K-means is asked for three clusters in the same measurement space, knowing nothing of species: pick three centres, assign each flower to the nearest, move each centre to the middle of its assignees, repeat until settled. Against the true species it scores an adjusted Rand index of 0.73 in the captured run, where 1.0 is perfect agreement and 0 is chance. The composition table explains the decimal: one cluster is purely setosa, all fifty, the geometry having found unaided what the tree’s first threshold found with labels; the other two clusters split the versicolor and virginica ranges untidily between them, because those species really do blur into each other in these measurements. Unsupervised evaluation argues from structure and usefulness rather than from a withheld answer key, a softer standard that the next chapter’s sealed losses will stiffen again.

title: 15  The Older AI in the Room
text:
15.4 What Each Branch Is For
The visit teaches a routing skill, of the same kind Chapter 12 fenced around typed judgments: given a problem, which branch of the family earns the first attempt?








Your material looks like
Reach first for
Because




A table of numbers, a label to predict
Decision tree or its ensembles; SVM beside it
Fast, inspectable, strong baselines, honest error bars


A table of numbers, no labels
k-means and kin
Structure and segments before anyone names them


Images, audio, signals with spatial or time shape
CNNs and deep nets (next chapter’s family)
Features must be learned from the raw grid, not hand-slotted


Language, instructions, messy documents, conversation
LLMs and this book’s wrappers
Meaning arrives unslotted; that is their whole trick



A support vector machine, the SVM in the first row, earns its mention as the classical classifier that draws the widest separating boundary it can between classes, the geometric opposite temperament to a tree’s axis-aligned questions; the notebook’s closing cell swaps it in on identical splits so you can compare held-out scores rather than temperaments in the abstract. Ensembles, forests of trees voting, are why the first row still wins tabular competitions against far larger machinery. The routing cuts both ways. Reaching for a language model to classify rows that already sit in clean numeric columns is usually an expensive way to get a worse, less inspectable answer. Conversely, hand-engineering feature columns for raw text is the 2010s version of the same mistake.

section: 15.5 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
text:
15.5 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
Two symmetrical cons run in this territory. The first relabels: a logistic regression or a gradient-boosted tree that has scored transactions well for a decade is presented, post-2023, as “our AI platform”, with the LLM era’s glamour borrowed for machinery that neither needs nor survives it. The second overreaches: an LLM demo classifies support tickets from raw text beautifully, and nobody mentions the tree over structured fields that would do most of the same job at a thousandth of the cost with rules a regulator can read. What model family is this, in the taxonomy rather than the brochure? Show me the held-out score and the mistakes, not the accuracy on data it trained on. If it is classical, which features carry the decision, and who chose them? If it is an LLM doing a table’s job, what did the table baseline score, and what does the difference cost per million rows?

15.7 Chapter Summary

AI is the umbrella; classical ML, deep learning, and LLMs are branches. This book’s first five parts occupy the LLM twig, and the title is earned narrowly and now explicitly.
Supervised classical learning runs fit, predict, evaluate on a sealed split. A decision tree on iris reaches 0.933 held-out accuracy in milliseconds and prints as rules a person can trace.
Unsupervised k-means finds geometric groups without labels; on iris it isolates setosa perfectly and blurs the overlapping pair, ARI 0.73.
Routing by material is the skill: tables to trees and SVMs, unlabelled tables to clustering, raw signals to deep nets, language to LLMs. Each branch misused on another’s material is a category error with an invoice attached.
The evaluation discipline (seal first, read mistakes, distrust training scores) is one continuous habit from this chapter through adapters.

title: 16  Train a Tiny Model
text:
16.1 The Concept First
Notebook companion: train_tiny_model.ipynb in the package repository’s notebooks/ folder. It runs on a laptop CPU in seconds at its defaults, or on a free Colab GPU if you prefer. This chapter narrates it; the notebook is the doing.
Misconception this chapter kills: “Training uploads knowledge into the model.” Training adjusts weights so next-token guesses score better on examples. What looks like knowledge later is that adjustment, generalised or memorised, and this chapter shows you the difference on a graph.
The build: a character-level model of 38,874 parameters, trained on ten sentences about this book, sampled before and after training, then overtrained on purpose.
Strip a language model to its training loop and four moves remain. Represent text as numbers, because arithmetic needs numbers: here, one integer per distinct character, the smallest workable tokenisation. Guess the next token everywhere in a batch of examples, with the current weights. Measure how wrong the guesses were with a loss, a single number that falls as guesses improve, computed here as cross-entropy, which you can read as average surprise at the true next character. Then nudge every weight a small step in the direction that would have reduced that loss on this batch, which is all gradient descent means here: follow the slope downhill, in small steps, many thousands of times.
Frontier training runs are those four moves at far larger scale, on trillions of tokens, with engineering beyond this book’s scope. But scale changes the behaviour that emerges, not the identity of the moves. A model that has only ever done this, whose entire education is guessing the next character slightly less badly each step, is the same kind of object whose call you have been making since Chapter 1. When a large model answers from its training in Chapter 5’s sense, this loop, on that text, is all the contact it ever had with the material.

title: 16  Train a Tiny Model
text:
16.2 Understanding Through Real Life
Think of learning a piano piece by playing it through against a score you can check note by note. Each pass, you hear where your fingers expected one note and the score had another, and your hands adjust a little. Play one short piece five hundred times and two different things can happen. You might learn the piece so thoroughly that related music gets easier, the fingering patterns generalising. Or you might merely memorise this one sequence, brilliant at these forty bars and helpless at bar one of anything else. From outside, during practice, both feel like improvement. The test that separates them is a piece you have not practiced.
Training loss is your accuracy on the practiced piece. Validation loss, computed on held-out text the trainer never trains on, is the unpracticed piece. Watching only the first number is how overfitting goes unnoticed.

title: 16  Train a Tiny Model
section: 16.3 The Build: Ten Sentences and a Sealed Test
text:
16.3 The Build: Ten Sentences and a Sealed Test
Open the notebook and run it cell by cell the first time. The corpus is ten sentences about this book (“the model proposes and the code disposes” and its friends), small enough that you can audit every word the model could possibly learn. Eight sentences form the training text; two are held out whole as the sealed validation set, the same discipline the LocoLabo capstone enforces on its training data. The notebook lets you prove why that whole-sentence split matters: split repeated text at a character offset instead and the same sentences appear on both sides, after which validation loss flatters you by measuring memorisation and calling it learning. Leakage of that kind, in larger datasets, is behind a share of published AI results.
Before training, the notebook samples from the fresh model. Keep the output. In the run captured for this draft, seeded for reproducibility, the untrained model produced this, starting from the characters the:
the ifolhpydttyctri.jfemckylhcr.dpkxu.fsdscouotlf x deorxxxaoxdyilatyle
That is what near-random weights sound like: the alphabet available, no preferences worth the name. Then 600 steps of training, which took about four seconds on the machine that captured this run:
step    0  train 3.322  val 3.350
step  100  train 1.500  val 3.027
step  200  train 0.606  val 4.477
step  300  train 0.413  val 5.260
step  400  train 0.332  val 5.553
step  500  train 0.248  val 5.862
step  600  train 0.233  val 6.154
At step 0 the model is equally surprised by everything, training and held-out text alike. Training loss then falls without pause, as expected. Validation loss rises almost from the start. The model is not learning English or even these sentences’ patterns in any general sense; it is memorising eight sentences with increasing fidelity, at the expense of the two it has never trained on. Sample it and the memorisation is audible: near-verbatim corpus sentences at low temperature, degrading gracefully as temperature rises and the sampler is allowed to choose less probable characters. Temperature, met here as a dial between conservative and adventurous sampling from the same weights, matters when hosted models expose it as a setting: it changes the choosing without changing the knowledge.
The notebook then overtrains deliberately, four times more steps, and the finishing figures in the captured run (training loss 0.153, validation 7.984) show the same pattern further along. Nothing malfunctioned: the optimiser did its job on the objective it was given, examples it was shown, and a corpus far too small to generalise from. Scale accounts for most of the difference between this small run and the models in Part I. The loop, the loss, the need for sealed evaluation, and the ease of lying to yourself with the wrong split did not vary with scale.

title: 16  Train a Tiny Model
section: 16.4 What This Buys You as a Reader
text:
16.4 What This Buys You as a Reader
You will likely never pretrain a model anyone uses, and neither will most professional builders of AI systems. The returns on this afternoon are conceptual, and they carry through the rest of Part VI and back into the earlier parts. Training data is now a concrete thing you have assembled and audited by eye, which changes how you read claims about what a model “was trained on”. Loss is a number whose two versions you have watched diverge, which is the permanent antidote to training-curve screenshots in vendor decks. And generation is demystified at the source: the fluent text of Part I is sampling from next-token scores at some temperature.
A one-layer, 38,874-parameter character model teaches the loop, not the capabilities: word-level tokenisation, depth, instruction tuning, reinforcement from feedback, and data curation at scale are each worlds this notebook gestures past. The notebook’s closing cell points at Karpathy’s Zero to Hero for the concepts taught properly and at nanochat, nanoGPT’s successor codebase (nanoGPT itself is now deprecated by its author), for readers who want this chapter at full size. Appendix D carries the same pointers in the exit map.

title: 16  Train a Tiny Model
section: 16.5 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
text:
16.5 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
“We trained our own model” spans everything from this notebook to a frontier run, and the sentence alone tells you nothing. Trained on what, how much of it, and who audited the corpus the way you just audited ten sentences? What was sealed for evaluation, and can I see validation beside training performance rather than a sample of outputs? Is this full training, continued training, or an adapter over someone else’s base, which is the next chapter’s distinction and the one most often elided in pitches? Look for answers that name data cards, splits, and held-out numbers.

text:
16.6 Practice Exercises
Exercise 16.1 (Level 1). Run the notebook untouched. Save the before-training sample, the loss table, and both temperature samples. Explain the validation column to an imaginary colleague in three sentences.
Exercise 16.2 (Level 2). Repeat with the leakage split the notebook warns about (one repeated text, cut at a character offset). Compare validation behaviour and state, in writing, which split you would trust for a result you intended to publish.
Exercise 16.3 (Level 3). Swap in your own small text, commit messages, a poem, your meeting openings. Hold out a sensible sealed slice for that genre and defend the split. What does the trained model capture, and what does it plainly not?
Exercise 16.4 (Level 4). Vary one setting at a time (model width, steps, learning rate) across three runs with the seed fixed. Record which moved validation loss and which only moved training loss. That table is your first hyperparameter intuition, earned cheaply.
Exercise 16.5 (Level 5). Write the data card for your tiny corpus as if for publication: source, size, split discipline, known biases, what a model trained on it should never be trusted to do. One page, suitable for attaching to the notebook.

title: 16  Train a Tiny Model
text:
16.7 Chapter Summary

Training is four moves on repeat: tokenise, guess next tokens in batches, measure surprise as loss, nudge weights downhill. Scale changes what emerges, not what the moves are.
A 38,874-parameter character model trained on eight sentences memorises them in seconds; sealed validation sentences expose the memorisation as training loss falls and validation loss rises.
Splits are methodology, not bookkeeping. Splitting repeated text leaks the test into training and makes validation lie politely.
Sampling temperature changes the choosing, not the knowledge.
This notebook is a teaching instrument: real pretraining adds tokenisation, depth, data curation, and post-training this chapter only names.

16.10 Next Steps
You have now trained a model from nothing and watched it memorise. Almost nobody in practice starts from nothing: they start from a capable base model and adjust its behaviour with a comparatively tiny amount of additional training. The next chapter does that with a LoRA adapter, your own examples, and the same sealed evaluation, and asks whether it actually beat the base.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
text:
17.1 The Concept First
Notebook companion: finetune_adapter_colab.ipynb in the package repository’s notebooks/ folder, distilled from the LocoLabo capstone training notebook your author supervises. It needs a free Colab GPU. Budget tens of minutes at this chapter’s scale, not the capstone’s hours.
Misconception this chapter kills: “Fine-tuning teaches the model our facts.” An adapter mostly learns from relatively few examples how answers should sound and behave here. Whether it beats the base model at anything is an empirical question with a sealed test, and the honest answer is sometimes no.
The build: a LoRA adapter over Qwen3-4B teaching one plain-English answering dialect, exported to Ollama, then judged blind against its own base model.
Almost nobody retrains a capable model from scratch to specialise it, for the arithmetic reason Chapter 16 made vivid: full training touches every weight, with the memory and compute to match. Fine-tuning starts from a pretrained base and continues the same next-token training on a small, deliberate dataset: examples of the behaviour you want more of, formatted as the conversations the model should learn to continue. LoRA, low-rank adaptation, goes one step thriftier. The base weights are frozen, and a small set of extra weights wired alongside key layers is the only thing trained: in the notebook’s configuration, well under one percent of the total parameter count. At serving time the adapter can be merged back into the base to produce one ordinary model file, which is what the notebook exports for Ollama.
The proportion governs what this technique can and cannot do. A fraction of a percent of movable weights, trained on dozens to hundreds of examples, is enough to shift voice, format discipline, refusal habits, and which of the base model’s existing knowledge gets foregrounded in a domain. It is a poor place to store a policy manual. Facts planted by fine-tuning arrive with no citation, go stale silently, and compete with everything else in the base, while Chapter 6’s retrieval supplies facts at question time with sources attached. The division of labour is therefore: retrieval for what is true, system prompts for what is cheap to state, and an adapter only for behaviour that examples teach better than instructions do.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
text:
17.2 Understanding Through Real Life
Think of accent coaching for an already fluent speaker joining a regional service desk. You do not reteach them the language. You give them fifty recorded calls that sound right for this desk: the greeting shape, the local terms, the calm way of saying no, and you drill until the habits are theirs under pressure. And you would not coach product prices into their accent, however many times they repeat them in training calls, because prices change next quarter and the information belongs on the screen in front of them, not in their muscle memory.
The measurement discipline matches too. You would not certify the coaching by replaying the practice calls. You would hold back calls the coach never used, have the newcomer handle them, and compare against how they sounded on day one, judged by the desk’s own standards.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
section: 17.3 The Build: Data First, Because Data Is the Build
text:
17.3 The Build: Data First, Because Data Is the Build
Open the companion notebook at Steps 3 and 4. The training format is JSONL, one conversation per line, user then assistant, and the notebook opens with a miniature built-in dataset teaching a single dialect, short plain-English answers, so the whole pipeline can be smoke-tested before your own data is at stake. Then come the checks: every line parses, turns alternate correctly, no assistant answer is empty, duplicate prompts are flagged, and training prompts are intersected with eval prompts to catch leakage by name. Read two examples by eye before any GPU wakes up, because the model will imitate the assistant column with total sincerity, typos, hedges, evasions, and all. In fine-tuning, the dataset’s quality sets your ceiling.
Two scaling notes separate the book build from the capstone it distils. The capstone demands at least 500 training examples and 50 sealed eval examples before a proposal is even approved, because its question is whether a domain adapter beats a 4B base in earnest. The notebook here builds 60 smoke-test records from four question-answer pairs repeated, which is enough to exercise every mechanism and nowhere near enough to claim a specialisation. Your real run sits between: 50 to 100 of your own examples with a sealed eval set you wrote before training, not after seeing results. Write the eval first. Chapter 11 required the same moderation before marks.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
section: 17.4 Train, Export, and Put It Back on the Bench
text:
17.4 Train, Export, and Put It Back on the Bench
The middle of the notebook is the LocoLabo machinery at book scale: Unsloth loads Qwen3-4B in 4-bit so a free GPU can hold it, get_peft_model attaches the LoRA layer to the attention projections, examples are rendered through the model’s own chat template (worth reading once, to see the exact markers the model trains on), and an SFT trainer runs three epochs at the recorded settings. Watch the loss with Chapter 16’s eyes: on a set this small it will head toward memorisation quickly, and the training loss is the rehearsal number, of interest mainly when it misbehaves. Then the merge: the notebook exports a quantised GGUF, roughly two and a half gigabytes, and the instructions walk it out of Colab before the session deletes it, a failure mode with its own graveyard of lost evenings.
Back on your machine the artefact rejoins the world of Part I. A one-line Ollama Modelfile (FROM ./your-file.gguf) registers it under a name, HANDS_ON_AI_MODEL points your earlier chapters’ scripts at it, and the department has a new intern whose only difference from the old one is the dialect you drilled. Nothing else in your stack changes: fine-tuning, done this way, is a change of model file, evaluated like any other model change from Chapter 4.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
section: 17.5 The Only Question That Matters: Did It Beat the Base?
text:
17.5 The Only Question That Matters: Did It Beat the Base?
Ask every sealed question of both models, the untouched base and your adapter, ideally with the answers shuffled and their sources hidden from whoever marks. Mark them against the criteria your dialect claims: plainness, brevity, format, whatever the adapter was for, using Chapter 11’s judge as the tireless marker and your own reading of a sample as the moderation. Report both scores and read some actual answers, not only the aggregate, because a point gained in style while losing a fact is visible only at reading distance.
At this scale, unfashionable outcomes are common. The adapter may win on voice and lose on substance, which says your examples taught manner at the expense of content. It may match the base everywhere, which usually says a system prompt would have bought the same shift for almost nothing, and Chapter 2 should be tried first next time. Or it may lose, through too few examples, too many epochs, or a dialect the base already spoke. The capstone this notebook descends from states its position in its brief, and this chapter adopts it whole: a negative result with a rigorous explanation is a better piece of work than a flattering number nobody can defend. Publish the training log either way; the log template travels with the notebook materials for that reason.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
text:
17.6 Extension: Learn from Preferences
Supervised fine-tuning imitates examples. Preference learning goes one step further and adjusts weights from comparisons: for the same prompt, this answer over that one. The simplest teachable form is DPO, direct preference optimisation, which consumes triples of prompt, chosen answer, and rejected answer and nudges likelihood toward the chosen style without a separate reward model to babysit. Your supply chain for pairs already exists in this book: generate two candidate answers per sealed-style prompt with your SFT model, rank them against your criteria (your marks first, the judge’s second, per Chapter 11’s order of trust), and file the winners and losers. The companion notebook’s closing section sketches the additional cells; treat them as a second sitting, not a first run.
Beyond DPO sits online reinforcement learning proper, GRPO being the current teachable shape: sample several answers, score them with a reward, push weights toward the better-scoring behaviour, repeat. It earns its complexity only where the reward can be computed: arithmetic checked by Python, formats validated by a parser, code judged by its tests. At inference time, simple reward-guided search exists, and you built it in Chapter 10: the ratchet changes no weights. In weights, the simple on-ramp is preferences offline and verifiable rewards online; beyond that lies a research programme. Each step up this ladder is judged by the same sealed set, untouched by SFT, DPO, and every threshold conversation in between.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
section: 17.7 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
text:
17.7 Where a Demo Can Mislead You
“Fine-tuned on our data” is a claim about a process, not a result, and it demos beautifully because style is the easiest thing an adapter changes and the first thing an audience feels. Ask for the base model’s score on the same sealed questions, the size and provenance of the training set, who wrote the assistant column and to what standard, and what the system does about the facts the adapter confidently absorbed wrong. Then ask the substitution question this chapter makes unavoidable: what here could retrieval or a system prompt not have done, cheaper and with citations? Look for answers that give behaviour examples and eval tables.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
text:
17.8 Practice Exercises
Exercise 17.1 (Level 1). Run the notebook’s data cells only (no GPU work): build the miniature dataset, run the checks, and deliberately introduce one malformed record, one duplicate, and one leaked eval prompt. Confirm each is caught by name.
Exercise 17.2 (Level 2). Write your sealed eval set first: ten questions with the answers your dialect should produce, marked against criteria you state now. Date the file. Nothing in training may touch it.
Exercise 17.3 (Level 3). Complete the smoke-test training run and export. Register the result in Ollama beside the base and ask both models three training questions and three sealed ones. Record where rehearsal and readiness diverge.
Exercise 17.4 (Level 4). Grow to your own 50-plus examples in a dialect you care about. Train, export, and run the blind comparison. Write the training log entry the capstone would expect, whichever way the result lands.
Exercise 17.5 (Level 5). Build preference pairs from your adapter’s sealed-set answers, ranked by your marks with the judge as second reader. Spec the DPO run (pairs count, epochs, what would make you stop) and the exact result that would convince you it beat SFT alone. Run it if the spec survives your own reading.

title: 17  Teach It a Dialect
text:
17.9 Chapter Summary

LoRA fine-tuning freezes the base and trains a small added layer, well under one percent of weights here, on conversation examples; merged and quantised, it serves as an ordinary Ollama model.
Adapters teach voice, format, and habits. Facts belong in retrieval, cheap instructions belong in system prompts, and the substitution question comes before any training run.
The dataset is the lesson: format checks, duplicate and leakage detection, and reading examples by eye precede the GPU work and matter more than the settings.
Success is defined against a sealed eval, base versus adapter, marked blind. A negative result, rigorously shown, is a legitimate and publishable outcome.
Preference learning extends the arc in order: ratchet search (no weights), DPO on ranked pairs, GRPO only with verifiable rewards. The sealed set judges all three.

Before moving on, ensure you:

Can state what your adapter is for in one sentence a system prompt could not achieve
Wrote your sealed eval before training and kept it untouched
Compared base and adapter blind, and read raw answers beside the scores
Logged settings, loss, and outcome, especially if the answer was no

Where did the adapter beat the base honestly, and where did it merely sound more like your examples?
Which behaviour in your working life is currently bought with a long system prompt that fifty examples might teach better?

17.12 Next Steps
Part VI ends where the book’s first page began, with a model call, except that you have now stood on both sides of it: directing pretrained models through their front door, and adjusting weights yourself at toy scale. The conclusion gathers all six parts into the single shape they share. Readers going deeper from here have two roads: Karpathy’s line for training itself, in Appendix D, and the LocoLabo capstone this chapter distilled, for adapter work done in teams on real domains.

title: 18  The Shape Underneath
text:
18.1 The shape, in six drawers
Package companion: all of hands-on-ai 0.6.0, which you have now read in the pieces that matter.
Misconception this chapter kills: “I need to learn a framework.” Frameworks will come and go above this shape. You now own the shape.
The build: none. This chapter assembles what you built into one picture and hands you the questions to carry out of the lab.
Almost every system in this book is one call to a model, wrapped in plain Python. The six parts were five families of wrapper plus, in the optional Part VI, a look at how the object inside the call is made. Each part killed the misconception that its wrapper was the intelligence:
Point at any AI product you use this week and the decomposition exercise from Chapter 1 now has six drawers to sort its behaviour into, the last one asking what the model itself was trained and adapted on. The chatbot is Part I with a budget. The document helper is Part II with better retrieval. The agent is Part III with a larger bench and higher stakes. The platform is Part IV with dashboards where your folders and logs were. The voice assistant is Part V wrapped around whichever of the earlier parts does its thinking. Products differ, sometimes enormously, in the quality and scale of their wrappers. Almost none differ in the underlying event: text, and now pictures and sound by conversion, assembled into a payload; a model call; the result checked, filed, or fed around again by code someone wrote on a Tuesday.

title: 18  The Shape Underneath
text:
18.2 The questions to carry
Each chapter ended by slowing a demo down, and the questions collect into a single habit. What did this add around the plain call? Where does the evidence come from, and can I open it? Who executes, on what allowlist, and what happens on the worst input? Where are the stage outputs, the traces, the logs, and which exit ended this run? Who marked the quality, against what criteria, calibrated against whose reading? Where did my words, pictures, and voice travel, and how long are they kept?
Models will be replaced under you quarterly; several already have been while this book was written. The wrappers will be renamed by vendors twice a year. The questions survive both, because they attach to the seams where someone’s code met a model call and a decision got made about evidence, authority, cost, or proof. Asking them of your own builds first is the difference between supervising AI systems and merely operating them, and it is the same difference this series’ other titles circle from their own directions: Conversation, Not Delegation for the thinking discipline, Speak Software for directing agents without code, Prove, Don’t Persuade for insisting on evidence over demonstration.

title: 18  The Shape Underneath
text:
18.3 Leaving the lab
This package was built to be outgrown, and its own philosophy says so without embarrassment: a learning lab, small on purpose, trading completeness for clarity so the concepts stay visible. The moment your needs name a gap here, error handling with real retries and budgets, streaming at scale, a vector store, judged evaluation over thousands of cases, agents running tools concurrently, voice with interruption handling, you have reached the exit it was aimed at, carrying the concepts a production framework will assume you have. Appendix D maps each module to its grown-up counterparts, and Ship Python, Orchestrate AI in this series takes the professional road in full: the same shapes, built to be operated by strangers.
One graduation exercise is worth doing before you shelve the lab. Pick the module you leaned on hardest and read its whole source in one sitting, pen in hand, answering for every function the question Chapter 1 taught you: what does this add to the plain call? The chat module will take an afternoon. So will the rest together. A reader who has done that once stops asking whether they are technical enough to judge an AI system, which was the quiet hope underneath the preface.

title: 18  The Shape Underneath
text:
18.4 Practice Exercises
Exercise 18.1 (Level 1). Choose an AI product you used this week and sort its behaviour into the six drawers, one line per drawer, naming what you are inferring rather than observing.
Exercise 18.2 (Level 2). Revisit your earliest learning journal entries. Find one belief about AI systems that a specific chapter’s build, not its prose, changed for you. Name the listing.
Exercise 18.3 (Level 3). Assemble two parts on one bench: a voice loop whose answers are grounded by your document index, or a judge watching your workflow’s draft stage. Keep it small; the composition is the exercise.
Exercise 18.4 (Level 4). Write the one-page version of this book for a colleague: the shape, the five questions, and the single exercise from any chapter that would teach the most in an hour. Defend your choice of exercise.
Exercise 18.5 (Level 5). Capstone. Build one small thing for real use, from Appendix C or your own backlog, under this book’s disciplines: stated criteria, a checkable goal, sources shown, errors visible, a budget. Ship it to one other person and record what their use taught you that your testing did not.

title: 18  The Shape Underneath
text:
18.5 Chapter Summary

Almost every system built here is one model call plus a wrapper: the call itself, grounding, action, control (typed judgments included), and the senses. Part VI adds where the weights inside the call come from, and how little of them an adapter moves.
The durable skill is seam questions: evidence, execution authority, traces and exits, calibrated quality, data travel and retention.
The package is a learning lab designed to be outgrown. Reaching its limits with the concepts intact is success, and Appendix D is the exit map.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.1 Running a Script
You do not need to read this appendix first. Each chapter names the Python it needs and points back here. Read the section you need, when you need it, and return to the chapter. Every example in this appendix is complete, runs without a model or a network, and prints exactly what is shown beneath it. Type them in rather than pasting.
If you want to learn Python itself, properly and for its own sake, that is a different book: Code Python, Consult AI in this series. After this appendix, no listing in this book will contain a construct you have not met.
A Python program in this book is a plain text file whose name ends in .py. You write it in any text editor, save it, and run it from a terminal:
Python reads the file from the top, line by line, and does what each line says, in order. When it reaches the end of the file, the program is over. There is no separate compile step; the first line is the start.
Lines beginning with # are comments. Python ignores them. Comments are notes for human readers, and in this book they often carry the listing number and the file name to save the code as.
First used in Chapter 1.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
python ask.py


# This line is a comment. Python skips it.
print("This line runs.")
This line runs.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.2 print: Showing a Value
print writes a value to the terminal. Getting a value and showing a value are different acts, and Chapter 1 makes you delete a print once to feel the difference.
print("Hello")
print(42)
Hello
42
The words Hello are inside quotation marks, which makes them text. The 42 has no quotation marks, which makes it a number. That distinction, text versus number, is the next two sections.
First used in Chapter 1.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.3 Variables: Named Values
A variable is a name attached to a value. The = sign attaches it. Read answer = "yes" as “the name answer now refers to the text yes”.
name = "Sam"
age = 31

print(name)
print(age + 1)
Sam
32
A variable can be reassigned, and the old value is gone. A variable can also hold the result of a calculation or, throughout this book, the text a model returned. Choose names that say what the value is: question, answer, and usage carry you through most of Part I.
First used in Chapter 1.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.4 Strings: Text
Text in Python is called a string: characters between quotation marks. Single and double quotes both work, and a string can contain the other kind of quote without trouble.
greeting = "It's working."
print(greeting)
print(len(greeting))
It's working.
13
len counts the characters, spaces and punctuation included. Two string operations appear constantly in this book. Adding strings with + joins them end to end. And an f-string, a string with the letter f before its opening quote, lets you drop values into the middle of text by naming them inside curly braces:
name = "Sam"
tokens = 53
print("Name: " + name)
print(f"{name} used {tokens} tokens.")
Name: Sam
Sam used 53 tokens.
Chapter 6 builds a prompt by assembling strings this way; f"..." there is an f-string like the one above.
First used in Chapter 1. F-strings first used in Chapter 6.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
section: A.5 Imports and pip: Borrowing Code
text:
A.5 Imports and pip: Borrowing Code
Python code written by other people is organised into packages. pip install downloads a package onto your machine once:
pip install "hands-on-ai==0.6.0"
An import line inside your script then borrows named pieces of that package for that run:
from hands_on_ai.chat import get_response

print(type(get_response))
<class 'function'>
Read the import as a path: inside the package hands_on_ai, in its chat section, find the thing called get_response. After that line, your script can use the name get_response as if you had written it yourself. If the package is not installed, Python stops at the import line with a ModuleNotFoundError, which is the error message’s way of saying the install step was skipped.
First used in Chapter 1.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.6 Calling Functions
A function is a named piece of work that takes inputs, called arguments, and hands back a result. You call it by writing its name followed by parentheses holding the arguments:
words = "the model sends text back".split()
print(words)
print(len(words))
['the', 'model', 'sends', 'text', 'back']
5
Arguments can be given by position, as above, or by name. A named argument spells out which input it fills, and named arguments can often be left out, in which case the function uses a default value chosen by its author:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}."

print(greet("Sam"))
print(greet("Sam", greeting="Welcome back"))
Hello, Sam.
Welcome back, Sam.
That example defines a function too, which is the next section. get_response(question, system="...") in Chapter 2 uses the same pattern: one argument by position, one by name, the rest left at their defaults.
First used in Chapter 1. Named arguments first used in Chapter 2.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
section: A.7 Defining Functions: Naming Your Own Work
text:
A.7 Defining Functions: Naming Your Own Work
The word def begins a function definition. The indented lines beneath it are the function’s body, and return sends a value back to the caller:
def add_tax(price):
    return price * 1.10

print(add_tax(20))
22.0
Indentation matters in Python. The four spaces before return are how Python knows the line belongs to the function. Most editors insert them for you when you press Tab after a line ending in a colon. If Python complains about indentation, check that every line of the body lines up exactly.
Chapter 2 wraps a system prompt in a function to make a bot. The function there does no arithmetic: it calls get_response and returns whatever came back.
First used in Chapter 2.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.8 Lists: Ordered Collections
A list holds values in order, inside square brackets, separated by commas:
roles = ["system", "user", "assistant"]
print(roles[0])
print(len(roles))
roles.append("user")
print(roles)
system
3
['system', 'user', 'assistant', 'user']
Counting positions in a list starts at 0, so roles[0] is the first item. append adds one item to the end. The message list in every payload in this book is a list, and Conversation in Chapter 3 spends its life appending to one.
First used in Chapter 1, where the printed payload’s messages value is a list.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.9 Dictionaries: Named Collections
A dictionary holds values under names, called keys, inside curly braces. Each entry is a key, a colon, and a value:
message = {"role": "user", "content": "What is my name?"}
print(message["role"])
print(message["content"])
user
What is my name?
You read a value out by giving its key in square brackets. Each message in a payload is a dictionary with two keys, role and content, and the usage report from Chapter 1 is a dictionary with three. Environment variables in Chapter 4 live in a dictionary called os.environ, which your code reads and writes the same way:
import os

os.environ["HANDS_ON_AI_MODEL"] = "llama3"
print(os.environ["HANDS_ON_AI_MODEL"])
llama3
First used in Chapter 1. os.environ first used in Chapter 4.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
section: A.10 Loops: Doing Something to Each Item
text:
A.10 Loops: Doing Something to Each Item
A for loop runs its indented body once per item in a list:
chunks = ["first chunk", "second chunk", "third chunk"]
for chunk in chunks:
    print("-", chunk)
- first chunk
- second chunk
- third chunk
The name chunk is a variable that takes each item’s value in turn. The body can do more than print. Chapter 6 loops over retrieved chunks to build one long prompt string, adding a line per chunk:
prompt = "Context:\n"
for chunk in ["alpha", "beta"]:
    prompt += f"- {chunk}\n"
print(prompt, end="")
Context:
- alpha
- beta
\n inside a string means a newline, the invisible character that ends a line. And += means “add this to the existing value”, so prompt += f"- {chunk}\n" grows the string a line at a time.
First used in Chapter 6.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
section: A.11 Objects and Methods: Verbs After a Dot
text:
A.11 Objects and Methods: Verbs After a Dot
Some values carry their own operations. You reach those operations with a dot, and an operation reached by a dot is called a method. You have already used two in this appendix: split on a string and append on a list.
Chapter 3 introduces the pattern at full size. Conversation(system="...") creates an object, a self-contained bundle holding a message list and a token total. The object is stored in a variable, usually chat. After that, chat.ask(...), chat.save(...), and chat.reset() call methods on that bundle, and chat.total_tokens reads a value stored inside it:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.total = 0

    def add(self, amount):
        self.total += amount
        return self.total

counter = Counter()
print(counter.add(5))
print(counter.add(3))
print(counter.total)
5
8
8
That is a complete, if tiny, class. Counter is the template, counter is one object made from it, and the object remembers its total between calls because the total lives inside the object. This book asks you to use two or three classes written by the package. The self you see repeated is how the object refers to its own stored values; you can read past it safely.
First used in Chapter 3.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.12 True, False, and None
Three special values appear throughout the book. True and False are Python’s yes and no, produced by comparisons and consumed by settings like return_usage=True. None means the absence of a value: no usage reported, no model chosen yet, nothing found in the cache.
usage = None
print(usage is None)
print(3 > 2)
True
True
When a listing checks if usage: before reading token counts, it is guarding against None. Chapter 1 explains the two ordinary situations where usage is None, and neither is an error.
First used in Chapter 1.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
text:
A.13 Reading an Error Message
Sooner or later Python will stop and print a traceback: several lines naming the file and line where things failed, ending with the complaint. Read tracebacks from the bottom. The last line says what went wrong. The lines above it say where. Three complaints cover most of what beginners meet in this book:








Last line begins
Usually means
First thing to check




ModuleNotFoundError
A package is not installed
Run the pip install step


NameError
A name was used before it existed
Spelling, or a missing import


SyntaxError or IndentationError
Python could not parse the file
The line it points at: quotes, colons, indentation



Errors from the model call itself are different. As Chapter 1 explains, get_response returns them as strings beginning with ❌ or ⚠️ rather than stopping your program, and handsonai doctor is the first tool for those.

title: Appendix A — Just Enough Python
section: A.14 A Worked Example Using Most of It
text:
A.14 A Worked Example Using Most of It
This script uses an import, a list of dictionaries, a loop, an f-string, and a function definition. It is the payload from Chapter 1, rebuilt from the pieces in this appendix, with no model involved:
import json

def build_payload(model, question):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": question},
    ]
    return {"model": model, "messages": messages}

payload = build_payload("llama3", "What is my name?")
for message in payload["messages"]:
    print(f'{message["role"]}: {message["content"]}')
print(json.dumps(payload))
system: You are a helpful assistant.
user: What is my name?
{"model": "llama3", "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "What is my name?"}]}
If that script reads as ordinary to you, you have enough Python for this book. Return to the chapter that sent you here.

When in doubt, run the doctor before touching code; it reads the same configuration your scripts will, in the same order.
Each row has a matching key in the config file (server, api_key, model, embedding_model, vision_model, stt_server, stt_model, tts_server, tts_model) for settings you want to survive terminal sessions. Environment variables still take precedence.

text:
B.2 The Free Local Path
Ollama covers chat, embeddings, and vision from one install at http://localhost:11434 with no account and no key. The pulls this book needs:
ollama pull llama3           # chat (Parts I to IV)
ollama pull nomic-embed-text # retrieval (Chapter 6)
ollama pull moondream        # vision (Chapter 13)
Audio is the local exception. Transcription and speech typically come from a small separate server that speaks the same /v1/audio/ dialect: speaches or whisper.cpp serving a Whisper model for speech-to-text, Kokoro or Piper for text-to-speech. Point HANDS_ON_AI_STT_SERVER and HANDS_ON_AI_TTS_SERVER at them and Chapter 14 works untouched. Local everything is the private, offline, per-call-free route; its costs are your hardware’s limits on model size and patience, felt most in Parts III and V.

title: Appendix B — Model Access
text:
B.3 Hosted Providers
Any service exposing the OpenAI-compatible chat and embeddings endpoints can drive most of the book through the three variables from Chapter 4. The package documentation carries worked examples; the shapes are uniform:
export HANDS_ON_AI_SERVER="https://api.openai.com"       # OpenAI
export HANDS_ON_AI_SERVER="https://openrouter.ai/api"    # OpenRouter
export HANDS_ON_AI_SERVER="https://api.groq.com/openai"  # Groq
export HANDS_ON_AI_API_KEY="your-key-here"
export HANDS_ON_AI_MODEL="the-provider's-model-name"
Audio and vision coverage varies by provider, so check the endpoints you need before a Part V weekend. Free tiers come and go and are deliberately not enumerated here; the package documentation and the providers are the live sources. One classroom pattern: one shared local or hosted server behind a key, the three variables issued to students, and the cache (below) warmed before the lesson so a network failure cannot fail thirty exercises at once.

Local calls cost time; hosted calls cost money per token. Either way, the shape of the spend per build is knowable in advance:

title: Appendix B — Model Access
text:
B.5 The Response Cache
Setting HANDS_ON_AI_CACHE to a directory turns on a plain-text reply cache for get_response: identical model, system prompt, and question return the stored answer without contacting a server, and with token usage reported as None. Warm it once for a classroom and reruns become reproducible, offline-capable, and free. Clear it by deleting the directory. Remember from Chapter 4 that it is also a folder of transcripts on disk, and that a model or prompt change does not invalidate old entries until the name inside the lookup changes. Note its scope: the cache sits in get_response, so direct Conversation turns and vision calls bypass it.

title: Appendix C — The Project Gallery
text:
C.1 After Part I: Chat
The hands-on-ai documentation hosts the project guides at michael-borck.github.io/hands-on-ai, organised by module. At version 0.6.0 there are 46 of them. Each guide assumes the concept and walks a build. The natural rhythm is chapter first, its named project second, then one or two neighbours from the same module while the ideas are warm.
The book’s companion builds were the five-line call, the personality bots, and the remembering conversation. The chat gallery is the largest, with 24 projects. Start with Build Your Own Personality Bot and Knowledge Quiz Bot, both direct extensions of Chapter 2’s function-wrapping pattern. Build Your Own Cache reimplements Chapter 4’s lesson from the inside. From there the gallery widens by appetite: tutors and journal bots for the patient, text adventures and debate panels for the playful, dashboards and converters for the practically minded. Any three will sharpen the system-prompt judgement from Chapter 2.

title: Appendix C — The Project Gallery
text:
C.2 After Part II: Retrieval
Four projects: My First RAG Bot, which Chapter 6 builds; PDF Question-Answering Chatbot, the same shape aimed at one document type; Build Your Own Q&A CLI, for readers who want the command-line tool rather than the library calls; and Hybrid Reasoning Bot, which starts mixing retrieval with the agent patterns of Part III. Do the first alongside the chapter and at least one more on documents you own.

title: Appendix C — The Project Gallery
text:
C.3 After Part III: Agents
Twelve projects, from Simple Calculator Agent (Chapter 7’s companion, with a longer treatment of safe expression evaluation) through Build Your Own Tool and Custom Tool Creator, to Multi-Tool Problem Solver and Agent Evaluation Framework at the deeper end. Heed Chapter 7’s caution as you browse: the registry calls tools with one string, so read each guide’s tool signatures before adopting them, and test tools directly before letting a model anywhere near them.

C.4 After Part IV: Workflow, Loop, Eval
Four projects across the three control modules, each named in its chapter: Build a Pipeline for workflows, Improve Until Good and Build a Ralph Loop for the two loop shapes, and Judge Your Bot for evaluation. These are short modules and the guides are close to the chapters; their value is repetition on material of your choosing, with the review gates, logs, and moderation habits intact.
