title: Appendix C — The Project Gallery
text:
C.6 Three Capstones
Pick by your reason for reading. Each composes at least three parts of the book.
For a personal tool. A document assistant over your own notes: Chapter 6 retrieval over a folder you maintain, Chapter 3 conversation for follow-ups, Chapter 11 criteria checking that answers stayed inside the documents. Success looks like a tool you open weekly whose sources you can click through to.
For a classroom demo. A judged improvement loop shown live: a rough student paragraph, Chapter 10’s ratchet with its log projected where the class can argue with each keep and discard, and a Chapter 11 moderation table comparing the class’s marks with the judge’s. Success looks like students disputing criteria wording, unprompted.
For a portfolio piece. A small staged workflow with traces kept: a Chapter 9 pipeline whose middle stage uses Chapter 7 tools and whose final stage is scored by Chapter 11’s judge, all outputs filed for inspection. Success looks like a stranger being able to replay the run, find the stage you are least proud of, and hear you explain its job card.

title: Appendix D — Going Deeper
text:
D.1 The Call Itself (Part I)
You will outgrow this package at a named moment: a budget it cannot express, a volume it cannot serve, an error it returns as a string where production needs a policy. Frameworks and services change quickly enough that this appendix names neighbourhoods and the current well-known residents, and trusts you to check who lives there when you arrive. The concepts are the durable part.
Your next step is the providers’ official SDKs, which add streaming, structured outputs, provider-native tool calling, and proper exceptions where this package returns error strings. If several providers must sit behind one interface in your own code, that is the job of routing layers such as LiteLLM, which generalise Chapter 4’s three variables into a managed surface. Carry with you: the payload is still the truth; read what any SDK actually sends before trusting its abstractions, as Listing 1.2 taught you.

title: Appendix D — Going Deeper
text:
D.2 Grounding (Part II)
Production retrieval adds vector stores, hybrid keyword-plus-vector search, metadata filtering, incremental reindexing, and evaluation sets for retrieval quality. LlamaIndex is the neighbourhood’s best-known framework address, with LangChain’s retrieval pieces and every vector database vendor nearby. Carry with you: it is still chunk, fetch, answer. The engineering is in chunking policy, freshness, and proving with scores and sampled answers that the fetch deserves the prompt built on it.

title: Appendix D — Going Deeper
text:
D.3 Action (Part III)
Agent frameworks such as Pydantic AI and the SDKs’ native agent tooling replace text-format parsing with validated function calling, add dependency injection for tools, retries with policy, and tracing as a first-class output. Carry with you: the model still only proposes. Your registry, your allowlists, and your worst-input discipline from Chapter 7 are the safety case, whatever the framework calls its decorators. Read Ship Python, Orchestrate AI in this series for this transition taken at professional length.

title: Appendix D — Going Deeper
text:
D.4 Control (Part IV)
Workflow engines and durable-execution platforms add scheduling, parallelism, persistence across crashes, and human-task queues where this book had folders and a person at a bench. Evaluation matures into dataset-driven evals: fixed case sets, regression gates in CI, judge ensembles with measured agreement. Carry with you: stage outputs you can inspect, goals stated before loops run, and moderation records for every judge. A platform that hides any of the three removes evidence you need. Typed judgments grow up into structured-output modes in the official SDKs, schema-constrained decoding in local servers such as Ollama (verify the current format behaviour before relying on it), and dedicated System One services such as TypeSafe’s Jev where calibrated probabilities are worth paying for.

title: Appendix D — Going Deeper
text:
D.5 The Senses (Part V)
Vision production work adds image pipelines, detection and OCR specialists beside the general VLM, and thinking about resolution and cost per image. Voice production is its own stack, and Pipecat is the front door the package’s final project points at: streaming transcription and synthesis, interruption handling, and the latency budget fought hop by hop. Carry with you: translators around a text core, and the consent and retention questions, which do not get simpler at scale.

title: Appendix D — Going Deeper
text:
D.6 The Model Itself
One door remains if the black box itself is what you want opened. Andrej Karpathy’s Zero to Hero series builds a small language model from first principles, at the cost of the mathematics Parts I to V promised to spare you: gradients, tensors, training loops. Its codebase line now runs from the deprecated nanoGPT to its successor nanochat, a full pretrain-to-chat pipeline kept deliberately hackable. Part VI opens this briefly, with toy training and a LoRA adapter; Karpathy covers it at full size. Nothing in Parts I to V requires either, and most builders of AI systems will never train a model.

title: Acknowledgments
text:
This book exists because the companion package came first. hands-on-ai began as a teaching lab: eight small modules, each wrapping one call to a model in plain Python, with documentation pages and project guides for readers to build against. The book is the narrative the package leaves out, the why and the progression and the misconceptions each module is designed to kill. Every listing here was checked against the package source, and the package is better for the checking; several sharp edges found while drafting these chapters, including a tool description that its own function could not accept, were worth finding in a manuscript rather than in a classroom.
The listings were tested the way the book asks readers to test them: offline first, with scripted stand-ins where a live model would only add weather, and against local models where the call itself was the lesson. Students and classes who worked through early versions of these builds, in applied AI teaching at Curtin University and in the workshops around it, showed exactly where the explanations ran ahead of the code. Where a chapter now slows down to print a payload or read a trace against the grain, it is usually because a room full of capable people skimmed past that step and then could not say what had happened.
The intellectual debts are named where they are incurred: the ReAct paper for the reason-act-observe loop, the original retrieval-augmented generation paper for search-then-prompt, Andrej Karpathy’s teaching for the go-deeper exits, and Conversation, Not Delegation for the argument that judging model output is the new literacy. The optional final part draws on the local fine-tuning community’s tooling and notebooks, credited in place.
The open-source community behind Quarto, Pandoc, Python and GitHub made it possible to write, build and publish this book from text files the reader can inspect, alongside the package it narrates. The local-model ecosystem, Ollama in particular, is what makes a book like this runnable offline in a classroom at all.
This book was written using the machinery it describes. AI drafted, summarised, checked listings and proposed structures at every stage, and produced fluent errors on schedule, which is why every printed output that claims to be program output was verified by running the program. The machine made the work faster. The judgement, and the responsibility for every claim that remains, are the author’s.

title: About the Author
text:
Photo of Michael Borck


Michael Borck is a software developer and educator working at the intersection of human expertise and artificial intelligence. He teaches applied AI and AI in business at Curtin University, and runs The Human Edge masterclasses through Curtin Executive Education. Build AI, Understand AI grew out of a simple classroom observation: students could use AI tools fluently long before they could say what those tools were doing, and the gap closed fastest when they built a tiny version themselves.
His earlier book, Conversation, Not Delegation, argues for treating AI as a thinking partner you converse with. Speak Software teaches readers to direct agents without writing code. This book opens the box those agents are built on: every chapter reduces one familiar AI system to a single model call wrapped in plain Python, built in miniature so it can be read in one sitting. The doing lives in the companion package, hands-on-ai (pip install hands-on-ai), whose modules, documentation and project guides this book narrates; neither duplicates the other.
The bet underneath the book is that models change every few months and the ideas underneath them change slowly. A reader who has built chat, retrieval, an agent loop, a workflow and a judge by hand stops being fooled by demos, whatever the next model is called. Michael builds educational software and resources, and writes about the 80/20 principle in learning and professional judgement.
